items.title: [sherringham.net] A Martian Odyssey
items.content_html:
Frontera
By Lewis Shiner

Shiner's first novel is not a long book (about 280 pages) but manages to fit in a lot of action and a surprising amount of character development. The driving motive of one of the main protagonists is even something that has been "programmed" into him; a motive that swirls with classic myth, pushing him forward in his own heroic tale. This is only one part of the book that makes it more interesting than some.

On Earth, a nuclear war has caused the collapse of nation states and their replacement by competing corporations, each vying for economic and technological control. The martian colonies have partly collapsed. Now we have a mission to the red planet, perhaps less to save the colonists and more to discover and seize some potentially important technology. The book paints the world (both Earth and Mars) in a satisfying patina of dust and decay. The technology is, just about, still working but increasingly fragile and R&D is as much a violent land grab than white-coated laboratory employment.

For a slim novel with multiple characters, Shiner does well to describe both a back story for each and a decent motivation. The tragedy of a colony left to fend for itself against a very hostile martian environment, and all that entails for both physical and mental health is brought to life in all its shabbiness. There is plenty of action and a few surprises. A minor complaint I would make (and this risks me being seen as a prude) are a couple of sex scenes I thought were a bit explicit, unnecessarily so. But nothing that detracted me from the overall enjoyment.

This is a novel I've seen rated highly - and I concur. Very readable and it reaches a great crescendo of excitement at the end.
